nameStory: Annual fleabane earned its unusual name from the old belief that these plants could repel fleas when dried and scattered around homes. The word 'fleabane' literally means 'flea poison,' though modern science shows these plants aren't actually effective flea repellents. The 'annual' part of the name refers to its short life cycle, completing its entire life in just one growing season.
description: Annual fleabane is a common wildflower that looks like a small, delicate daisy with tiny white petals surrounding a yellow center. This herbaceous plant typically grows 1-4 feet tall with a branching, somewhat scraggly appearance. It produces dozens of small flower heads clustered at the tops of its stems, creating a cloud-like display of miniature daisies. Despite being called 'annual,' it can sometimes live for two years, making it technically biennial in some cases.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny daisy-like flower heads about 1/2 inch across with numerous narrow white petals (actually ray petals) surrounding bright yellow centers. The petals feel papery and thin to the touch, and dozens of flower heads cluster together in branching groups at stem tips.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves with toothed edges that feel slightly rough and hairy when rubbed between your fingers. Lower leaves are larger and may have short stalks, while upper leaves are smaller and attach directly to the stem without stalks.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in an open, branching pattern with multiple stems spreading outward from the base. The overall shape is somewhat irregular and weedy-looking, not forming a neat, compact clump like garden flowers.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces fluffy, dandelion-like seed heads with tiny seeds topped by white, feathery bristles called pappus. These seeds blow away easily in the wind and feel silky when touched.

habitat: Annual fleabane thrives in disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, old fields, and garden edges throughout New England. It prefers sunny spots with well-drained soil and readily colonizes areas where the ground has been recently disturbed. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species in meadows, pastures, and waste places from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of toothed leaves close to the ground. Early spring growth is often hard to distinguish from other young weedy plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, when the distinctive small white daisy-like flowers appear in abundance. This is the best time for identification when flowers are fresh and numerous.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming into early fall, gradually replaced by fluffy seed heads. Seeds disperse on fall breezes, and the plant begins to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only dried brown stems. Seeds remain dormant in the soil until the following spring's germination.

funFact: Each tiny flower head can produce up to 100 microscopic seeds, and a single annual fleabane plant can generate over 10,000 seeds in one growing season - that's enough seeds to potentially cover a football field with new plants!
confusionNotes: Annual fleabane is easily confused with daisy fleabane, but annual fleabane has wider, more obvious white petals and tends to be taller and more robust. Remember: 'Annual = Abundant petals' - the white ray petals on annual fleabane are more noticeable and substantial-looking than the thread-thin petals of daisy fleabane.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's always annual, this plant can actually be either annual or biennial depending on growing conditions and when seeds germinate. The scientific name was recently changed from Aster annuus to Erigeron annuus as botanists refined the classification of daisy-family plants.
compareHints: Among New England fleabanes, annual fleabane is distinguished by its relatively wide, obvious white petals and robust growth habit. Daisy fleabane has much more thread-like, sparse petals, while Philadelphia fleabane typically has pink or purplish petals. Horseweed lacks the showy petals entirely, having only tiny greenish-white flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its showier cousins like daisy fleabane and annual fleabane, horseweed has extremely small, inconspicuous flowers that barely look like typical daisy-family blooms.
Among its fleabane relatives, robin's plantain stands out as the earliest bloomer with the most robust appearance and widest petals.
Daisy fleabane differs from its fleabane cousins by having the narrowest ray petals - they're almost thread-like compared to the broader petals of annual fleabane or Philadelphia fleabane.
Among New England's fleabanes, Philadelphia fleabane stands out with its extremely numerous thread-like petals (50-150) compared to daisy fleabane's fewer, broader petals (typically under 50).
Unlike the much more common daisy fleabane and annual fleabane which form branching clusters of many small flowers, hyssop-leaved fleabane usually produces just one flower head per stem.
Coulter's fleabane differs from common New England fleabanes by having fewer but larger flower heads and more robust growth.
